value: a response was recorded for 67% of looms, 50% of overhead passes and 35% of blank-screen controls
method: freely moving animals in a small tank (15 x 25 x 15 cm) under a backlit screen shown an expanding dark disc (loom, 10 to 70 deg over 0.5 s), an overhead pass (70 deg circle moving across the screen) or a blank white screen; response (sudden jerks of the arms or raising of the dorsal-most spines) scored from video by five blind observers; Bayesian model with stimulus type fixed and animal and observer random
conditions: 14 wild-collected adults (Isla Solarte, Panama), 3-day recovery in open-air aquaria; 36 videos scored: 14 looms, 14 overhead passes and 8 blank-screen controls; each animal saw the loom first, after 4 min under a plain white screen, and the overhead pass second, after a further 4 min (order as described, not stated to be randomised), each once; how, when and from which animals the 8 blank-screen control videos were made is not stated; the paper does not say every video was scored by all five observers; light and time of day for this tank are not given; response timing not recorded; observers also marked a 'response' in 35% of blank-screen control scorings, the baseline against which the model tests the stimuli; the next Results sentence reads 'The model found that animals respond to both loom and overhead pass stimuli but not to a negative control (Fig. 2).'; the loom-pass difference is confounded with presentation order; the percentages cannot be whole-video counts (67% of 14 is not an integer), so they are probably pooled over the five observers (70 scorings per moving stimulus, 40 for controls; my inference, not stated in the quote); the model reported in the following Results sentence put the probability of a response above control at over 99% for looms and 96% for overhead passes (read from the fetch summary, not the quoted sentence); daytime irradiance in the size experiments was 379 +/- 291 W m-2 (not measured for the loom tank)

method: larvae approached from the front by a hand-held dissecting pin with a 1.1 mm spherical head; a larva counted as responding if it moved before being touched, too fast for one video frame (0.03 s), with no swimming for 0.17 s before the probe moved; responsiveness analysed in 3 mm size classes by weighted linear regression
conditions: treatment light-strep: neuromasts made non-functional with streptomycin (5 mmol/l; drug side effects on other systems not tested in the text read), added 5 min before testing (block not verified in these larvae; the authors cite earlier work that streptomycin ablates superficial neuromasts and spares the inner ear, so hearing remained), tested in light (30 uE m-2 s-1; dark trials <0.01 uE m-2 s-1 under infrared), two larvae per Petri dish; per-treatment larvae numbers (61, 90 and 89 in the unit's reading) not confirmed against Table 1; the range is across size classes with no ontogenetic change (P = 0.26) and a slope different from light-control larvae (P = 0.002); comparison groups in the same Results section: dark-strep (neither neuromast nor visual input) responded in 0 to 7% (fetch summary of a longer sentence), and light-control larvae rose from 57% at 5 to 7 mm TL to 100% at 20 mm; lab-reared larvae from NMFS Beaufort Laboratory embryos, 20 to 22 C, salinity 29 to 31 per mille; larvae not stated to be reused; response to the probe does not separate vision from any residual non-neuromast sense, and the probe was approached by hand; dark-control larvae (neuromasts intact, no light) did not differ significantly from light-controls (P = 0.42), and only 3 dark-strep larvae responded in all
